summary:
I've been putting most of my recent hours into a fleet monitoring dashboard for my home lab (four boxes — a server, a dev host, a media box, and an AI workstation). I skipped the obvious move of grabbing Prometheus or Grafana off the shelf and wrote an agentless SSH collector instead: a stdlib-only Python script gets piped over stdin to each host every 30 seconds, no daemon installed, no sudo. Metrics land in a generic `(timestamp, host, metric, label, value)` table in SQLite, so a new metric type — disk temps, GPU wattage, whatever — never needs a schema change, and the retention ladder (raw for a week, 5-minute buckets for 90 days, hourly after that) keeps mins and maxes instead of just averaging them away, because a 447-watt spike smeared into a 178-watt mean is exactly the fact you'd want to keep.

The part I'm more proud of is what it refuses to report. Power-state metrics on one box are meaningless because that machine is supposed to run its RAM full, so I swapped in a pressure-stall metric instead of raw occupancy. Link speed gets checked against what a NIC is rated for, not just "up or down" — one host sat pinned at 100 Mb/s on a gigabit port for hours and nothing caught it under the old model. And cron jobs get reported as "fired" or "missed," never "succeeded," because the collector genuinely can't prove success and I'd rather it say nothing than lie confidently.

On the GPU side, I run a shared Tesla P100 across several workloads — an image generator, a couple of local LLM backends, a roleplay-model server — that can't coexist in 16GB of VRAM. I built a small FastAPI proxy that sits in front of all of them, and before it forwards a request to whichever backend needs the card, it evicts everyone else and polls memory until it's actually free. The gnarliest bug there was a deadlock: one caller acquired the GPU lease under the wrong client name, which caused the proxy to evict the very service that was trying to acquire it, and that service's acquire call was synchronous inside its own event loop — so the whole thing went dark, CPU usage near zero, no errors, just silence, until the lease timed out on its own.

Smaller thing that shipped this month: a viewer for months of power-draw logging on that same workstation, since the data existed but nobody had actually looked at it. It draws real gaps as gaps instead of interpolating across a 15-day logging outage, and leads with a staleness banner — because the outage itself is the kind of thing a dashboard should surface, not paper over.

highlights.oneLiner: FastAPI proxy serializing a shared GPU across backends; fixed an eviction deadlock this month
